messages.subject: GRF approximation
parts:
Dear all,

I am having a presentation on Monday about the SPDE link between GRF and GMRF.

In the slide attached I wrote down how I interpret the low-dimensional representation of the spatio-temporal GRF. 
Could you tell me if I am right, that in my case \tilde{z} is the GMRF or is the whole expression \sum from j=1 to N \psi_j(s,t)\tilde{z}_j the GMRF?

Sorry for this stupid question.

I am very much looking forward to your answer.
All the best,
Corinna

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] GRF approximation
parts:
Since you use Q=Q_T x Q_s, you are using a tensor product space-time
basis, with each \psi_j(s,t) being the product of a spatial basis
function and a temporal basis function,
and you impose a product-separable precision/covariance structure on
the process.
Assuming you're basing the model on Markov models in both space and
time, then your space-time process is Markov both in the continuous
domain and with respect to the basis weights, assuming the temporal
basis functions are also local in time.
With non-local basis functions, the Markov property would only hold
with respect to a graph with a dense set of edges, which usually isn't
called Markov (even though strictly speaking it is; the Markov
property is always expressed in relation to some "neighbourhood
system/topology")

So your \tilde{z} vector is a discrete domain GMRF, but the underlying
infinite/continuous domain SPDE is also a GMRF with respect to the
continuous domain; when the SPDE operator is of integer order, a
continuous Markov property holds.

The finite dimensional sum psi_j(s,t) z_j expression isn't quite the
full SPDE process, but rather a finite rank approximation of it.
However, that's _also_ a Markov process here; it's piecewise
conditionally deterministic.

The class of GMRF models is just a subset of GRF processes; _Every_
GMRF is a GRF.
Some of the literature is a bit confused on this point, and we didn't
even have the full picture in the 2011 SPDE/GRMF paper. The full
theory can be found in the books/papers by Rozanov (1970s/ early 80s).

Finn

parts:
Dear Finn,

thank you for your answer. Really appreciate it.

Maybe one more question: As in the paper with you, Cameletti and others from 2011, I want to use the state-space model for my geostatistical data.
However, I read the paper a couple of times and still don't fully understand.

In my equation (3) z_t is assumed to be a spatio-temporal GF with AR(1) dynamics which are represented in eq. (4).
Why do I model these "innovations" w_t with a purely spatial Matern covariance? What are innovations?

Well then I can represent my innovations w_t as a GMRF field with w_t~N(0,Q_S^(-1)). Ok. But then my z_t will also become a GMRF which can be substituted by my Finite Element representation which I posted above. Right?
But in Cameletti it seems differently. There \xi=(xi_1^prime,....xi_T^prime) forms a GMRF (with no explanation about xi_t^prime) and finally you rewrite B\xi_t. So would B in this case be the observation matrix for my finite element representation with \sum psi_(s,t)?

Hope I did not formulate too many questions in one.

Thank you very much, 
Corinna

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] GRF approximation
parts:
"In my equation (3) z_t is assumed to be a spatio-temporal GF with
AR(1) dynamics which are represented in eq. (4).
Why do I model these "innovations" w_t with a purely spatial Matern
covariance? What are innovations?"

The short answer is "because it's convenient/easy to construct that model".
In any AR(1) model we write
z_{t+1} = a z_t + w_t
and w_t are sometimes called "innovations" because they describe
what's "new", after taking the scaled version "a z_t" of "z_t".
In the spatial setting, we need a spatial model for these w_t fields,
and since we know how to construct Matern fields, that's just an easy
choice to make.

Because of the "separable" nature of the AR(1) space-time model, we
can take the regular AR(1) 1-dim "time" Q_T precision, and the spatial
Q_S precision (from the spatial Matern model), and get the space-time
precision as
Q_T \otimes Q_S.

The B in B\xi_t is the observation model matrix, yes. It contains the
evaluated product-basis functions for the space-time basis, at the
observation locations.

Finn
